paragraphs.heading: What a field is
paragraphs.text: In mathematics, a field is a set where you can add, subtract, multiply and divide, and those operations work just as they do for the rational numbers. The most familiar fields are the rational numbers, the real numbers and the complex numbers. Fields are basic building blocks, used across algebra, number theory and many other parts of mathematics.

paragraphs.heading: The rules of a field
paragraphs.text: Formally, a field is a set F with two binary operations, called addition and multiplication. A binary operation takes any ordered pair of members of F and gives back exactly one member of F. The two operations must obey the field axioms: both are associative and commutative, and multiplication distributes over addition, so a ⋅ (b + c) = (a ⋅ b) + (a ⋅ c). There must be two different elements 0 and 1 with a + 0 = a and a ⋅ 1 = a. Every a needs an additive inverse −a with a + (−a) = 0, and every a other than 0 needs a multiplicative inverse a⁻¹ with a ⋅ a⁻¹ = 1.

paragraphs.heading: Subtraction and division for free
paragraphs.text: Those inverses are what make the other two operations possible. Subtraction is defined as a − b = a + (−b), and division as a / b = a ⋅ b⁻¹. Dividing by zero is ruled out by the definition itself. The rational numbers show how this works: each is a fraction a/b built from two integers, with b ≠ 0, the additive inverse of a/b is −a/b, and when a ≠ 0 its multiplicative inverse is b/a.

paragraphs.heading: Complex numbers as a field
paragraphs.text: Multiplying two complex numbers gives (a + bi)(c + di) = (ac − bd) + (bc + ad)i, which has the same form again, and so the complex numbers form a field. You can picture each complex number as a point in the plane, or as an arrow from the origin with a length and an angle. Adding two of them then means joining their arrows into a parallelogram. Multiplying is less obvious: the angles add and the lengths multiply, so the arrow turns and stretches.

paragraphs.heading: Where fields are used
paragraphs.text: Any field can supply the scalars for a vector space, the usual general setting for linear algebra. Branches of analysis rest on fields that carry extra structure, and basic theorems there depend on the structural properties of the real numbers. Number fields, close relatives of the rational numbers, are studied closely in number theory, while function fields help describe the properties of geometric shapes. Finite fields are used in error-correcting codes and cryptography. The real and complex fields turn up throughout mathematics, physics, engineering and statistics.

paragraphs.heading: Settling ancient puzzles
paragraphs.text: In ancient times, several geometry problems asked whether certain numbers could be constructed with only a compass and straightedge. Field theory is a key part of the proofs that trisecting an angle and squaring the circle are impossible using just those two tools. Galois theory, which studies the symmetries of field extensions, gives a neat proof of the Abel–Ruffini theorem: the general quintic equation cannot be solved in radicals.
